\section{Three Scenarios for the Lending Environment}
\label{sec:scenarios}

% Every number is read from thesis/chapters/generated/tab_scenarios.tex, tab_switches.tex,
% tab_cooloff.tex or tab_cap.tex, or from results/summary/results_numbers.json, all generated by
% notebooks/scripts/build_results_tables.py from results/raw; nothing is typed.

This section answers RQ3: how bureau visibility and mandatory affordability screening change simulated borrowing and distress, with and without peer influence on adoption.
We compare three scenarios.
The benchmark is the pre-2026 position, in which \ac{BNPL} obligations are invisible to the bureau and \ac{BNPL} requests pass only a light screen.
Under bureau visibility ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{bur}}$), \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's Regulation 23A test.
This is the affordability channel of the reported 2026 arrangements \cite{businessday_bnpl_2026}; their scoring channel is outside the model (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}).
Under mandatory affordability screening ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{aff}}$), the Regulation 23A test is applied to each \ac{BNPL} request, the South African analogue of the \ac{FCA}'s proportionate affordability check \cite{fca_ps26_1, woolard2021}.
A fourth arm runs the two switches together, to test whether either changes the effect of the other.
Every arm is run at $\beta = 0$ and at $\beta = 1$ (Equation~\ref{eq:peer}).

The light screen in the benchmark is a modelling assumption.
Whether an agreement that levies late fees is incidental credit, and which provisions of the \ac{NCA} would then apply, is a legal question that the scenarios do not settle (Section~\ref{sec:background}).

Tables~\ref{tab:scenarios} and~\ref{tab:switches} and Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios} report the outcomes.
Each scenario has its own seed block, so each difference is scenario less benchmark at the same $\beta$ and carries one unpaired standard error.
We report cumulative volume beside default because it separates two kinds of rule: one that only delays borrowing within the horizon leaves volume unchanged, while one that prevents borrowing lowers it.

Neither switch changes default detectably, alone or with the other.
Bureau visibility changes default by $+0.04 \pm 0.10$ points at $\beta = 0$ and $+0.09 \pm 0.12$ at $\beta = 1$.
Screening changes it by $-0.02 \pm 0.10$ and $-0.09 \pm 0.13$ points, and the two together by $+0.05 \pm 0.10$ and $-0.09 \pm 0.11$.
With standard errors of up to 0.13 points, only a change larger than about 0.25 points would exceed two standard errors, and a true change of that size would be missed about half the time.
The switches may have smaller effects, in either direction, that this design cannot detect.

Bureau visibility changes lending without a detectable change in default.
Once \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the Regulation 23A test, the traditional lender refuses more applications, 1{,}395 against 1{,}191 at $\beta = 0$, and grants R4.87 million in place of R5.46 million.
Cumulative \ac{BNPL} volume is also $5.1 \pm 1.4$\% lower at $\beta = 0$, although the switch does not act on \ac{BNPL} requests.
The 90+ day arrears share among credit-active households does not change detectably ($+0.14 \pm 0.13$ points at $\beta = 0$).
These outcomes are population aggregates, so they do not show what becomes of the households that are refused.

Mandatory screening refuses \ac{BNPL} requests that the light screen would grant.
Holding at the final tick falls from 17.64\% to 15.74\% at $\beta = 0$ and from 66.79\% to 63.96\% at $\beta = 1$, and cumulative volume is $5.3 \pm 1.3$\% lower at $\beta = 0$ and $1.5 \pm 0.3$\% lower at $\beta = 1$.

The screening test already sees the household's \ac{BNPL} instalments on every platform (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}), so adding bureau visibility to screening gives the platforms no new information.
Its effect falls on the traditional lender, which with both switches refuses about 100 more applications at $\beta = 0$ than under screening alone and lends about R0.3 million less.
With both switches, \ac{BNPL} volume is $6.7 \pm 1.3$\% below the benchmark at $\beta = 0$, and default does not change detectably.

Two features of the model may explain why neither switch changes default detectably.
First, a \ac{BNPL} agreement is small beside the room that the Regulation 23A test allows.
Each platform limits a household to a tenth of its monthly income and the mean want-driven purchase is R633, so adding these instalments to the test can change the decision only for households already close to the limit.
Second, the test assesses affordability at origination on the household's surveyed income, whereas sustained distress in the model follows income shocks that outlast the household's buffer (Section~\ref{sec:results-robustness}).
A test applied when credit is granted cannot see a shock that arrives later.
Both are explanations after the fact; neither is tested directly, because the outcomes do not follow the screened households.

Peer influence raises holding, volume and default in every scenario.
Default is 0.46 to 0.58 points higher at $\beta = 1$ in the three scenarios, and 0.40 points higher with both switches.
The comparisons give no evidence that peer influence alters the effect of either switch, although the design could not detect an interaction smaller than about 0.3 points.

Appendix~\ref{app:levers} reports two further levers, each run at both values of $\beta$.
The first is a cooling-off window that blocks want-driven purchases for one to four ticks after a want-driven purchase (Table~\ref{tab:cooloff}).
The second is a cap on the number of platforms a household may owe, which is hypothetical because no jurisdiction imposes one (Table~\ref{tab:cap}).
A household at the cap is refused every new agreement until a balance clears, so a cap of one allows one agreement at a time.
At $\beta = 0$ neither lever changes default detectably, although a cap of one removes 40.1\% of volume.
At $\beta = 1$ the window lowers default by between $0.28 \pm 0.08$ and $0.39 \pm 0.12$ points, and caps of one and two lower it by $0.31 \pm 0.12$ and $0.32 \pm 0.10$ points.
Cumulative volume in these arms is between 31.8\% and 76.3\% lower.
A cap of three does not change default detectably.

Every lever that lowers default detectably also removes about a third or more of borrowing, and does so only where peer influence is present.
The experiments do not show that the lost volume causes the fall in default.
In a diagnostic run at $\beta = 1$, a cap of two that counts agreements in place of platforms removes 32.9\% of volume and changes default by $-0.11 \pm 0.07$ points, which is not detectable (Appendix~\ref{app:levers}).
Bureau visibility and screening remove between 5\% and 7\% of volume at $\beta = 0$ and under 2\% at $\beta = 1$.
No lever was run under the alternative borrowing rules of Table~\ref{tab:effect}, so the dependence of these results on those rules is untested (Section~\ref{sec:amount}).
The model also has no measure of what a household loses when a purchase or a shortfall loan is refused.

In answer to RQ3, bureau visibility and mandatory screening change who is granted credit and how much is borrowed, and neither changes default detectably through the affordability channel, with or without peer influence.
